title: A Cottage in the Town That Wouldn't Claim Her
standfirst: Fern Coppedge painted this cottage in the village she had lived in since 1920, across the road from the teacher who helped make Bucks County's landscape painters a movement. For a decade the touring exhibitions that carried that movement's name around the country left her off the list — and even now, the museum built on its history can't agree on whether she was ever formally in the group.

sections.heading: Coat, Canvas, Tree
sections.body:
In November 1933, New Hope Magazine described watching Fern Coppedge do what she did every winter: [trudging through deep snow](https://www.buckscountyherald.com/opinion/history-lives/history-lives-fern-coppedge-artist/article_caaaa658-ff68-11ef-9ce2-8bc452f30d4c.html) wrapped in a bearskin coat, a family heirloom carried east from Montana, sketching materials slung over her shoulder. When wind threatened the canvas, she tied it to a tree. When the cold got worse than that, she [removed the back seat of her car](https://bucksco.michenerartmuseum.org/artists/fern-i-coppedge/) and painted from inside it instead, the glass down just far enough to see. She worked until her fingers stopped answering her.

One critic summed up the dedication by writing that, [born a man, she undoubtedly would have manned a trawler](https://bucksco.michenerartmuseum.org/artists/fern-i-coppedge/) and sailed the Arctic Ocean. It was meant as a compliment. It also says plainly what praise for a woman painter still had to sound like in Bucks County in the 1920s and 1930s: not that she painted well, but that she painted like a man would have had to, to earn it.

sections.heading: Across the Road from Her Own Teacher
sections.body:
She had trained for exactly this. In New York she studied under William Merritt Chase at the Art Students League; in Philadelphia, at the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts, her teacher was Daniel Garber, already a name in the Bucks County colony that would later be filed under Pennsylvania Impressionism. She had married Robert Coppedge, a science teacher, on 2 January 1904, in a marriage that lasted forty-four years; Robert painted too, as an amateur, and by every account backed his wife's ambitions rather than competing with them.

She first visited the New Hope area in 1917 and settled three years later in Lumberville — this cottage's own village — buying a converted 1773 Quaker meeting house barely across the road from Garber's own property. She did not leave Bucks County again until she died.

sections.heading: A Group That Can't Agree She Was In It
sections.body:
In 1916 a cluster of Bucks County landscape painters organised themselves for a purpose entirely to do with exhibitions: touring, as a set, to museums well beyond Pennsylvania. Over the following decade the New Hope Group sent work to something like thirteen shows around the country, building the reputation that eventually got attached to the whole colony. According to Alan Goldstein, guest curator of a recent exhibition on Coppedge, she [was ignored and rejected](https://www.yahoo.com/news/fern-isabel-coppedge-know-hope-030038693.html) by that circuit and kept off all thirteen shows — a colony, in his reading, guarding its Impressionist purity and, not incidentally, its status as a male club.

The record does not fully back him up, or fully contradict him either. The colony's own historical society lists Coppedge among the New Hope Group's ten founding members in 1916. The Michener museum's database, on its own page for Garber, gives a shorter, six-name roster that leaves her out, and calls her only an [informal](https://bucksco.michenerartmuseum.org/artists/daniel-garber/) associate of his. Two specialist sources, describing the same nine years, cannot even agree on who was in the room.

sections.heading: Purple in the Snow
sections.body:
Coppedge painted snow the colour she actually saw in it, not the colour convention expected. [People used to think me queer](https://www.ferncoppedge.com/biography.html), she said, because she saw deep purples and reds and violets in a field of snow. The art historian Arthur Edwin Bye, cataloguing the wider school, noted that she filled her landscapes with [houses and churches, lanes, bridges, and canals](https://bucksco.michenerartmuseum.org/artists/fern-i-coppedge/) — but it was the colour, not the subject matter, that set her apart from Garber, Redfield and the rest.

That colour sits uneasily with the label this feature files her under. Her early work was Impressionism in the ordinary sense: shimmer, light, observed colour. What she painted from the 1920s on moved further — flatter, more deliberately arranged, closer to Post-Impressionism than to anything Chase or Garber had taught her. She was not copying the snow in front of her. She was rearranging it.

sections.heading: The Show That Let Her In, and the One Sixty Years Later
sections.body:
Whatever the touring circuit did or didn't do, Coppedge was present when Bucks County's artists built something of their own closer to home. In November 1929 the Phillips' Mill Community Association bought its mill for $5,000, and among the [founding artists](https://www.phillipsmill.org/about/history) at its first exhibition — 125 works by 41 painters — was Fern Coppedge, alongside Garber, Redfield, Folinsbee and Mary Elizabeth Price. She had also, by then, been showing since 1922 with the Philadelphia Ten, an all-women exhibiting group she stayed with for thirteen years — one answer, among several, to a colony that would not fully claim her.

The writer James Michener, whose name the local museum now carries, put the general problem more bluntly than any curator has since. He said he [could not see](https://bucksco.michenerartmuseum.org/artists/fern-i-coppedge/) Garber, Lathrop and Redfield bothering much with women on a serious note. Coppedge died in New Hope in April 1951, aged sixty-seven, and asked for a plain memorial; her ashes went into the Delaware. It took the same museum until 1990 to give her a retrospective of her own — and it called her, in its own title, A Forgotten Woman.
